newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Power Beat tests car emission scrubber.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Power Beat tests car emission scrubber.

text.p: Power Beat International says it has found a revolutionary way of turning pollutants into fertiliser, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Wednesday.
The Hamilton-based technology company said it had successfully tested a practical "scrubber" system designed to clean hydrocarbon and other emissions from motor vehicle exhaust gases.

Power Beat managing director Peter Witehira releasing details of the system, said in a statement the company's approach could result in a significant reduction in air pollution throughout major cities of the world.
The company has for some time been studying various options available in terms of environmental and energy efficient vehicles.
But Witehira said the company's research found electric and hybrid vehicles were not a viable solution to motor vehicle air pollution problems.

He said Power Beat engineers believed the answer lay first in the development of a highly efficient internal combustion engine and an ultra lightweight urban vehicle which incorporated self-scrubbing technology. Such a vehicle would ideally run on natural gas or other suitable combustible fuels.

Power Beat has designed what it says is the world's first fully extruded internal combustion engine and parallel research led the company to developing a new exhaust scrubbing technology for motor vehicles. It says the technology was capable of producing zero emissions.
The scrubber captures exhaust particles, including carbon and nitrogen, using continuously cycled water. The water includes certain biodegradable catalysts and is screened through paper filters.

The company says tests show hydrocarbon emissions were reduced to 31 parts per million, half that of conventional catalytic converters, and to zero parts per million when used in series with an existing catalytic converter.
After up to eight hours of driving, or each time a vehicle needs refuelling, the paper filter cartridge is removed and dropped into a compost bin.
A new filter is then clipped into the vehicle's scrubber.
The company says the resultant fertiliser can then be sold to farmers or gardeners.
It says changing filters can take about 30 seconds and costs up to $1 per filter.
Power Beat intends licensing the technology.

The company is running a standard 1600cc van with one of the prototype exhaust scrubbers. A retrofit version is under development for some vehicle types such as taxis, buses and service vehicles. The company is also studying a process to allow automatic loading and unloading of the paper filter.
"The addition of fragrances to the scrubber catalyst adds a pleasant smell," said Witehira.
"We can provide any scent such as apple, lemon or even Chanel No 5 to add a touch of class to the clean exhaust discharge."
